deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is the first page of a printed offprint of Riemann's posthumous fragment 'Mechanik des Ohres'. It was published by J. Henle and E. Schering in Henle and Pfeufer's Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, 3. Reihe, Bd. 29 (1867). A handwritten note on the page gives this citation and replaces the struck-through printed subtitle 'Aus dem Nachlass von B. Riemann'.

The page carries three marks:
- the Göttingen library stamp ('Ex Bibliotheca Regia Academ. Georgiae Aug.');
- pencil shelf or number marks, including 'XVIII', which matches the number of this piece in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876);
- a red marginal annotation next to the footnote.

Content:
- Section 1, 'Ueber die in der Physiologie der feinern Sinnesorgane anzuwendende Methode', is a methodological statement. Beyond the general laws of nature, the physiology of a sense organ needs two special foundations:
  - a psychophysical one: the empirical determination of what the organ achieves;
  - an anatomical one: the investigation of its structure.
- Hence there are two routes to knowing the organ's functions. One can start from its structure and derive the laws governing how its parts interact. The next page continues: or one can start from its performance and seek to explain it. These are the synthetic and analytic routes, named after Newton and Herbart.
- The editors' footnote (Schering, Henle) says:
  - Riemann took up the theory of the hearing organ in his last months, prompted by Helmholtz's theory of tone sensations.
  - Section 1 and most of section 2 were left as a fair copy; the end of section 2 (from p. 13) was assembled from scattered drafts.
  - Riemann's remark opposing Helmholtz's theory of the ear's movements would only have become clear through his own full treatment.
  - From his conversations, the editors suspected that the disagreement would have arisen over how sound vibrations are transmitted to the cochlea, which Riemann treated as a hydraulic problem.

There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically.

results.what: Methodological framing of sense-organ physiology: two foundations (psychophysical and anatomical) and two routes (synthetic: from structure to function; analytic: from observed performance to an explanatory hypothesis).
results.modern_name: Forward modelling vs. inverse problem / hypothetico-deductive method in physiology
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's own published fragment 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867), reprinted in his Gesammelte Werke (1876)

results.what: Editorial report that Riemann disagreed with Helmholtz on the mechanics of the ear and treated sound transmission to the cochlea as a hydraulic problem.
results.usually_credited_to: Hydrodynamic cochlear models are usually traced to later work (e.g. Peterson & Bogert 1950, von Békésy); Riemann's remark is known from this published footnote

deep.surprise_reason: This is the printed, published offprint of a well-known posthumous Riemann text, included in his Collected Works. It contains no mathematics, only methodological prose and the editors' footnote, all long in the public record.
transcription_corrections: The handwritten journal name appears as 'Pfeuffer's' in the hand. The correct name of the journal's co-editor is Pfeufer (Karl von Pfeufer).
The pencil marks at the top read roughly 'X X±' (struck or erased) and 'XVIII' (struck). 'XVIII' corresponds to the number of 'Mechanik des Ohres' in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke.
The red vertical marginal annotation beside the footnote is only tentatively 'Henle!'; it is hard to read.

The handwritten citation reads in full: '(Aus Henle und Pfeufer's Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, dritte Reihe, Bd. 29)'. It replaces the struck-through printed line 'Aus dem Nachlass von B. Riemann¹)'.
